title: Reverse Engineer Anything Project Brings AI Agents to Binary Analysis
gist: REA, an open-source project with over 200K GitHub stars, uses MCP servers to let coding agents like Claude Code and Codex drive Ghidra, Hopper, and IDA for binary analysis, with demos of byte-exact function reconstruction. Reactions range from skepticism about its added value to fears it will undermine indie software protection and push big tech toward cloud-only delivery.

themes.theme: REA: agent-driven binary analysis via MCP

insights.claim: Reverse Engineer Anything (REA), an open-source project with over 200K GitHub stars, connects coding agents such as Claude Code and Codex to reverse-engineering tools like Ghidra, Hopper, and IDA.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Rapid adoption signals strong developer demand for AI agents applied to specialized security/analysis tooling.
insights.quote: Reverse Engineer Anything (REA) is an open-source project with over 200K GitHub stars that connects coding agents such as Claude Code and Codex to reverse-engineering tools like Ghidra, Hopper, and IDA.
insights.locator: Reverse Engineer Anything (REA) is an open-source

insights.claim: REA uses MCP servers to expose disassemblers to AI agents, letting them inspect functions and cross-references, trace program behavior, and iteratively test hypotheses against a binary; it runs locally and does not claim to recover original source code.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: MCP is becoming the integration layer that turns niche expert tools into agent-accessible capabilities.
insights.quote: REA uses MCP servers to expose reverse-engineering tools to agents
insights.locator: REA uses MCP servers to expose

insights.claim: REA's GitHub showcases include reconstructing a DX-Ball sound-panning function with tests matching all 3205 original x86 cases and all 63 compiled function bytes, tracing Notion's Electron clipboard implementation, and recovering bullet-ring angle calculations from 16-bit DOS code of Touhou 4.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Byte-exact reconstruction demos suggest AI agents can faithfully recreate compiled logic, eroding the protection binaries offer.
insights.quote: reconstruct a sound-panning function from the classic game DX-Ball with tests matching all 3205 original x86 cases and all 63 compiled function bytes

insights.claim: Besides native disassemblers, REA supports static analysis of JavaScript/Electron applications and .NET assemblies, and that JavaScript and .NET inspection can run without a native analysis engine.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Lowers the barrier to inspecting widely distributed desktop apps built on Electron and .NET.
insights.quote: JavaScript and .NET inspection can run without a native analysis engine.
insights.locator: REA is not limited to Ghidra

insights.claim: Some Hacker News practitioners question what REA adds beyond simply asking an AI coding agent to install and use Ghidra, the NSA-developed open-source tool, while others report better results than their previous attempts at agent-driven reverse engineering.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Thin-wrapper risk: value may accrue to underlying agents and tools rather than integration projects.
insights.locator: On Hacker News, some practitioners question

themes.theme: Strategic consequences for software business models

insights.claim: AI-assisted reverse engineering could accelerate big tech moving apps to the cloud, because shipping no binaries cuts off one channel of reverse engineering.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Could push vendors further toward SaaS/cloud delivery to protect IP, favoring cloud providers.
insights.quote: I feel this is going to accelerate big tech moving apps to the cloud, at least one channel of reverse engineering will be cut off if there are no binaries.
insights.locator: Hacker News user revelationnow writes instead

insights.claim: Independent developers on Reddit fear AI-assisted reverse engineering will make it easier to copy their games and applications, bypass paid features, and commercially exploit their work without permission.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Weakens moats of distributed-binary software, especially for indie games and apps relying on client-side paywalls.
insights.locator: On Reddit, some independent developers fear

insights.claim: An AMD director argues the industry has shifted from software being king and hardware a commodity to hardware being king and proprietary software becoming increasingly replaceable.
insights.speaker: Sreekanth Pannala
insights.so_what: Supports a thesis favoring hardware owners over proprietary-software vendors as AI makes code easier to replicate.
insights.quote: We’ve gone from an era when software was king and hardware was a commodity to one where hardware is king and proprietary software is becoming increasingly replaceable.
insights.locator: Sreekanth Pannala, director at AMD, notes

insights.claim: REA is released under the permissive MIT license for legitimate reverse engineering, research, and reconstruction, placing responsibility on users to obtain authorization and comply with applicable laws.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Legal liability shifts to users, leaving IP-enforcement risk unresolved for software owners.
insights.quote: Users are responsible for obtaining the necessary authorization and complying with applicable laws.
insights.locator: Released under the permissive MIT license

insights.claim: A LinkedIn commentator warns that AI-enabled reverse engineering sits on a murky ethical boundary and that tools built to help people tend to end up being used against them.
insights.speaker: Cleverson Santos
insights.so_what: Signals potential regulatory and reputational backlash around AI reverse-engineering tools.
insights.quote: That is a murky boundary! I don't view crossing those lines favorably—and this is just the beginning
insights.locator: Cleverson Santos, creator of the Persistent Intelligence Project
